metadata.title: Top US National Parks
metadata.description: A curated ranking of the top 15 national parks in the United States based on visitation, iconic status, biodiversity, scenery, and accessibility.

factors.name: Visitation
factors.description: Annual visitor count as reported by the National Park Service

factors.name: Iconic Status
factors.description: Cultural recognition, photography, and global name recognition

factors.name: Biodiversity
factors.description: Number of plant, animal, and ecosystem types within the park

factors.name: Scenery
factors.description: Landscape variety, geological features, and visual impact

factors.name: Accessibility
factors.description: Infrastructure, ADA compliance, road access, and gateway airports

rankingMethodology.dataSource: NPS annual statistics, IUCN species records, and visitor survey data

parks.name: Yellowstone
parks.overview: The world's first national park, Yellowstone sits atop a supervolcano and contains more than half of Earth's geothermal features—over 10,000 hydrothermal sites including geysers, hot springs, mud pots, and fumaroles. Its vast wilderness supports the largest bison herd in the US and thriving populations of wolves, bears, and elk.

best_seasons.notes: Summer offers the best road access and wildlife viewing. May and September are less crowded with mild weather. Most roads close November through April.

must_see_features: Watch Old Faithful erupt—approximately every 90 minutes
Hike to the rim of Grand Prismatic Spring for the aerial rainbow view
Dawn wildlife patrol in Lamar Valley for wolves and bison
Walk the boardwalk at Norris Geyser Basin
View the Lower Falls from Artist Point

trails.name: Grand Prismatic Overlook
trails.notes: Best aerial view of the spring

trails.name: Mount Washburn
trails.notes: 360° panoramic views, bighorn sheep sightings

trails.name: Fairy Falls
trails.notes: 197-ft waterfall with Grand Prismatic view

trails.name: Shoshone Lake Trail
trails.notes: Backcountry permit required; remote geothermal lake

wildlife.notes: Yellowstone holds the only continuously wild bison herd in the US. Keep 100 yards from bears and wolves, 25 yards from other wildlife.

entrance_fees.notes: America the Beautiful annual pass ($80) covers all NPS fee areas.

parks.name: Grand Canyon
parks.overview: One of the Seven Natural Wonders of the World, the Grand Canyon stretches 277 miles long, up to 18 miles wide, and more than a mile deep. The canyon's layered bands of colorful rock represent nearly two billion years of Earth's geological history. The Colorado River continues to carve it deeper each year.

best_seasons.notes: Spring and fall are ideal—mild temperatures and manageable crowds. Summer inner-canyon temperatures regularly exceed 110°F. The North Rim is open mid-May through mid-October only.

must_see_features: Sunrise or sunset from Mather Point or Yavapai Point
Hike partway down Bright Angel Trail
Drive or walk the Rim Trail between overlooks
Ranger-led geology talks at Yavapai Geology Museum
Visit Desert View Watchtower for panoramic canyon views

trails.name: Rim Trail
trails.notes: Paved sections; wheelchair accessible portions; spectacular views throughout

trails.name: Bright Angel Trail to 1.5-mile rest house
trails.notes: Only hike down as far as you plan to hike back; inner canyon heat is dangerous

trails.name: South Kaibab to Skeleton Point
trails.notes: No shade; stunning views; start before dawn in summer

trails.name: Bright Angel to Phantom Ranch (rim to river)
trails.notes: Overnight trip; permit and reservation required

wildlife.notes: Do not feed wildlife. California condors nest in the canyon—report any tagged birds to rangers.

entrance_fees.notes: Fees valid for 7 days. America the Beautiful pass accepted.

parks.name: Yosemite
parks.overview: Yosemite Valley's towering granite cliffs, roaring waterfalls, and ancient giant sequoias have inspired artists, photographers, and conservationists for over a century. The park shelters 800+ species of plants, 400+ bird species, and iconic landmarks like El Capitan and Half Dome that define the American wilderness ideal.

best_seasons.notes: Yosemite Valley requires a timed-entry reservation May–September. Waterfalls peak in late April to early June. Fall brings colorful foliage and far fewer crowds.

must_see_features: View El Capitan and Half Dome from Tunnel View at sunrise
Hike to Yosemite Falls viewpoint
Stand among the giant sequoias in Mariposa Grove
Drive or take the shuttle to Glacier Point for a valley panorama
Watch rock climbers on El Capitan at El Cap Meadow

trails.name: Valley Floor Loop
trails.notes: Flat paved and dirt loop; great for cycling or leisurely walking

trails.name: Yosemite Falls Trail
trails.notes: Climbs 2,700 ft; best in spring when falls are fullest

trails.name: Half Dome via cables
trails.notes: Permit required May–Oct; cables up final granite dome; physically demanding

trails.name: Sentinel Dome
trails.notes: 360° panoramic views; one of the most scenic short hikes in the park

wildlife.notes: Use bear canisters or park-provided bear boxes for all food. Black bears are active—do not approach or feed them.

entrance_fees.notes: Timed entry reservations are required peak season ($2 reservation fee). America the Beautiful pass accepted.

parks.name: Zion
parks.overview: Zion's towering red and white sandstone cliffs rise above the winding Virgin River, creating one of the most dramatic canyon landscapes in North America. The park is famous for narrow slot canyons, technical canyoneering, and the celebrated Angels Landing summit with its chain-assisted ascent.
highlights: The Narrows (slot canyon hike in the Virgin River)

best_seasons.notes: Spring and fall are ideal. Summer is extremely hot in the canyon (100°F+). Flash flood season July–September makes The Narrows dangerous. Crowds peak in summer; spring is busiest overall.

must_see_features: Hike The Narrows upstream through the Virgin River
Summit Angels Landing (permit required) for canyon panoramas
Walk to Lower and Middle Emerald Pools
Ride the free park shuttle through Zion Canyon Scenic Drive
Drive the Zion-Mount Carmel Highway through tunnels and switchbacks

trails.name: Riverside Walk
trails.notes: Paved; leads into The Narrows; wheelchair accessible to a point

trails.name: Canyon Overlook
trails.notes: Best views for minimal effort; starts just east of the long tunnel

trails.name: Angels Landing
trails.notes: Permit required; chain-assisted final ascent; exposure to heights; not for acrophobes

trails.name: The Narrows
trails.notes: Full one-way route requires permit; wetsuit rental recommended in spring/fall

wildlife.notes: California condors roost on canyon walls—look up! Keep distance from all wildlife.

entrance_fees.notes: Private vehicles prohibited on Zion Canyon Scenic Drive—use the free shuttle. America the Beautiful pass accepted.

parks.name: Grand Teton
parks.overview: Grand Teton's dramatic skyline—a jagged 40-mile wall of peaks rising abruptly from the Jackson Hole valley floor—provides some of the most photogenic mountain scenery in North America. The park lies adjacent to Yellowstone and shares a rich wildlife ecosystem with moose, wolves, and bears.
highlights: Snake River Overlook (Ansel Adams photo site)

best_seasons.notes: Summer offers full trail access and wildlife activity. September has golden aspen groves and reduced crowds. Winter allows snowshoeing and Nordic skiing. Most facilities closed November–May.

must_see_features: Photograph Snake River Overlook at sunrise or golden hour
Take the ferry across Jenny Lake and hike to Hidden Falls
Drive to Mormon Row and photograph the Moulton Barn with the Tetons behind
Spot moose at Willow Flats near Jackson Lake Lodge at dawn or dusk
Summit Grand Teton (technical climb with guide recommended)

trails.name: Jenny Lake Loop
trails.notes: Flat lakeside trail; ferry shortcut available

trails.name: Hidden Falls & Inspiration Point
trails.notes: Take the ferry to Hidden Falls; climb to Inspiration Point overlook

trails.name: Cascade Canyon
trails.notes: Stunning canyon with wildlife; connects to South Fork or North Fork

trails.name: Paintbrush Divide Loop
trails.notes: Backcountry permit required; one of the finest loops in the Tetons

wildlife.notes: Moose are extremely common around Willow Flats and along the Snake River. Give all large mammals at least 100 yards of space.

entrance_fees.notes: Combined pass with Yellowstone available. America the Beautiful pass accepted.

parks.name: Glacier
parks.overview: Called the 'Crown of the Continent,' Glacier National Park preserves over a million acres of pristine wilderness on the US–Canada border. The park holds 25 active glaciers (down from 150 in 1910), 700+ miles of trails, and exceptional biodiversity including grizzly bears, wolverines, and mountain goats.

best_seasons.notes: Going-to-the-Sun Road typically opens fully in late June–early July and closes mid-October. Vehicle reservations required July–September. Winter access limited to lower valleys.

must_see_features: Drive Going-to-the-Sun Road from west to east at sunrise
Hike to Grinnell Glacier before it disappears completely
Spot mountain goats at Hidden Lake Overlook near Logan Pass
Explore Many Glacier by kayak or rowboat
Watch grizzly bears digging for glacier lily bulbs in late June

trails.name: Hidden Lake Overlook
trails.notes: Starts at Logan Pass Visitor Center; mountain goats nearly guaranteed

trails.name: Highline Trail
trails.notes: One-way along the Continental Divide; exposed ledge at start; shuttle back from The Loop

trails.name: Grinnell Glacier
trails.notes: Boat shortcut available; one of the few remaining accessible glaciers

trails.name: Iceberg Lake
trails.notes: Icebergs float in the lake into August; grizzly bear country—bear spray required

wildlife.notes: Glacier has one of the highest grizzly densities in the Lower 48. Bear spray is strongly recommended on all trails.

entrance_fees.notes: Going-to-the-Sun Road vehicle reservations required July–September ($2 fee). America the Beautiful pass accepted.

parks.name: Rocky Mountain
parks.overview: Rocky Mountain National Park encompasses stunning alpine scenery that spans from montane forests to tundra above treeline. Trail Ridge Road, the highest continuous paved road in the US at 12,183 ft, crosses the Continental Divide and opens the alpine world to all visitors. The park is a stronghold for elk, moose, and bighorn sheep.
highlights: Trail Ridge Road (highest continuous paved road in the US)
Bear Lake and surrounding trail network
Longs Peak (14,259 ft, highest in park)
Hallett Peak views from Dream Lake

best_seasons.notes: Timed entry reservations required May–October. September is spectacular for elk rut in Moraine Park. Trail Ridge Road typically open late May through October.

must_see_features: Drive Trail Ridge Road to Alpine Visitor Center and walk on the tundra
Watch the elk rut at Moraine Park in September at dawn
Hike to Emerald Lake through Bear Lake, Nymph Lake, and Dream Lake
Spot bighorn sheep on Horseshoe Park near the Fall River entrance
Summit Longs Peak (permit required July–Sept) for ultimate Colorado experience

trails.name: Bear Lake to Emerald Lake
trails.notes: Most popular trail network; accessible; mountain reflections in each lake

trails.name: Alberta Falls
trails.notes: Quick waterfall hike; great for all fitness levels

trails.name: Flattop Mountain
trails.notes: Access to the Continental Divide; great alpine views

trails.name: Longs Peak Keyhole Route
trails.notes: 14er; permit required July–Sept; start by 3 AM to avoid afternoon lightning

wildlife.notes: Elk are highly visible in Moraine Park during the September rut. Stay 75 feet from elk, especially bulls during rut.

entrance_fees.notes: Timed entry reservations ($2) required May through October. America the Beautiful pass accepted.

parks.photo_credit: Photo: NPS / Rocky Mountain National Park

parks.name: Acadia
parks.overview: Acadia is the only national park in New England, protecting stunning coastal and mountain scenery on Mount Desert Island and the surrounding coast. The park blends rocky shoreline, ocean views, and pink-granite summit ridges in one of the most accessible and beloved park experiences on the East Coast.
highlights: Cadillac Mountain (first place in the US to see the sunrise, October–March)
Carriage roads (45 miles of gravel, car-free roads)

best_seasons.notes: October is spectacular for fall foliage. Summer brings lush greenery but also peak crowds. Timed sunrise reservations for Cadillac Mountain required May–October.

must_see_features: Watch sunrise from Cadillac Mountain summit (reserve your spot in advance)
Walk the ocean path from Sand Beach to Thunder Hole to Otter Cliff
Bike the historic carriage roads (bike rentals available in Bar Harbor)
Eat Jordan Pond House popovers with a view of The Bubbles
Photograph Bass Harbor Head Lighthouse at golden hour

trails.name: Ocean Path
trails.notes: Flat, paved coastal walk with sea spray, tide pools, and dramatic rock faces

trails.name: The Beehive
trails.notes: Iron rung ladder scramble; stunning ocean views; not for acrophobes

trails.name: Precipice Trail
trails.notes: Highest-rated technical trail in park; iron rungs and exposed ledges

trails.name: Cadillac Mountain South Ridge
trails.notes: Best hiking route to the summit; pink granite underfoot; sweeping coastal panoramas

wildlife.notes: Harbor seals frequent the rocky shores. Whale-watching boats depart from Bar Harbor for humpback and finback whales offshore.

entrance_fees.notes: Cadillac Summit Road reservation required sunrise–9 AM, May–October ($6/vehicle). America the Beautiful pass accepted.

parks.name: Olympic
parks.overview: Olympic National Park is one of the most ecologically diverse parks in the system, encompassing temperate rainforests, wild Pacific coastline, alpine meadows, and glaciated peaks—all within a single park. The Hoh Rain Forest receives up to 14 feet of rainfall per year, creating moss-draped forest of unparalleled lushness.
highlights: Hurricane Ridge (alpine meadows with Olympic Mountains)
Ruby Beach and Rialto Beach (wild Pacific coast)

best_seasons.notes: The park is accessible year-round, with different experiences each season. Rainforest visits are beautiful year-round. Hurricane Ridge may require tire chains October–April. Coastal areas are spectacular in winter storms.

must_see_features: Walk the Hall of Mosses at Hoh Rain Forest
Drive to Hurricane Ridge for mountain views and wildflower meadows
Walk along Rialto Beach or Ruby Beach at low tide for sea stacks and tide pools
Swim or kayak in the impossibly blue Lake Crescent
Soak in the Sol Duc Hot Springs surrounded by old-growth forest

trails.name: Hall of Mosses
trails.notes: Most famous trail in the park; ancient big-leaf maples draped in moss

trails.name: Hoh River Trail
trails.notes: Flat old-growth trail to Blue Glacier base camp (backcountry permit needed beyond Glacier Meadows)

trails.name: Hurricane Hill
trails.notes: Panoramic Olympic Mountains views; wildflowers mid-July

trails.name: Seven Lakes Basin Loop
trails.notes: Premier backcountry loop; permit required; elk and alpine lakes

wildlife.notes: Olympic is home to the Olympic elk subspecies found nowhere else. Coastal tide pools teem with purple sea urchins, sea stars, and anemones.

entrance_fees.notes: 7-day pass. America the Beautiful pass accepted.

parks.name: Great Smoky Mountains
parks.overview: Great Smoky Mountains is the most visited national park in the US, and for good reason—it is free to enter, easily accessible from the Eastern Seaboard, and harbors greater tree diversity than all of northern Europe. The ancient, misty Appalachian peaks support 19,000+ documented species including salamanders, black bears, fireflies, and wildflowers.
highlights: Clingmans Dome (6,643 ft, highest point on the Appalachian Trail)

best_seasons.notes: October peak fall foliage draws enormous crowds. The synchronous fireflies event in June requires advance lottery ticket. Spring wildflowers (April–May) are spectacular. Park is free to enter year-round.

must_see_features: Drive the 11-mile Cades Cove loop for white-tailed deer, black bears, and historic homesteads
Walk or drive to Clingmans Dome for sunrise above the clouds
Hike to Alum Cave Bluffs in spring for wildflowers
Experience the synchronous fireflies display in Elkmont (lottery required)
Walk a short section of the Appalachian Trail from Newfound Gap

trails.name: Laurel Falls
trails.notes: Paved trail to the most visited waterfall in the park

trails.name: Alum Cave Trail to summit
trails.notes: To Mt. LeConte summit; dramatic rock features along the way

trails.name: Chimney Tops
trails.notes: Rocky summit scramble; closed periodically for restoration

trails.name: Appalachian Trail from Newfound Gap
trails.notes: Begin on the AT at 5,046 ft; walk as far as you wish toward Charlie's Bunion (8 miles round-trip)

wildlife.notes: The park has ~1,500 black bears. Bears are frequently seen in Cades Cove and along roadsides. Stay 50 yards from bears and 25 yards from other wildlife. No entrance fee.

entrance_fees.notes: Great Smoky Mountains is one of the few major parks with NO entrance fee. Parking tags ($5/day or $15/annual) are required at many trailheads.

parks.photo_credit: Photo: NPS / Great Smoky Mountains NP

parks.name: Arches
parks.overview: Arches contains the greatest density of natural stone arches in the world—over 2,000 catalogued arches in just 76,000 acres of red-rock desert. Iconic formations like Delicate Arch (on Utah's license plate) and Landscape Arch (the longest in North America at 290 ft) draw photographers and hikers from around the globe.
highlights: Landscape Arch (longest arch in North America)
The Windows section (multiple arches in a small area)

best_seasons.notes: Spring and fall are ideal with moderate temperatures. Summer temperatures regularly exceed 100°F and the park implements timed-entry. Winter can bring snow that creates stunning red-and-white photos.

must_see_features: Hike to Delicate Arch at sunset for the classic silhouette photo
Walk the Windows Loop to see four major arches in two miles
Take the Fiery Furnace ranger-led tour (reservation required)
Photograph Landscape Arch in the Devils Garden area
Stop at Balanced Rock for an easy iconic photo opportunity

trails.name: Balanced Rock
trails.notes: Flat loop around the famous formation; quick stop

trails.name: Windows Loop
trails.notes: Visits North and South Windows and Double Arch; sandy but mostly flat

trails.name: Delicate Arch
trails.notes: Exposed slickrock; hot in summer; stunning at sunset; bring plenty of water

trails.name: Devils Garden Primitive Loop
trails.notes: Full loop visits 8 arches including Landscape Arch; requires scrambling

wildlife.notes: Desert bighorn sheep are regularly seen near the Delicate Arch viewpoint. Cryptobiotic soil crust (black, lumpy soil) is alive—step only on rock or sand.

entrance_fees.notes: Timed-entry reservations required April–October ($2 fee). America the Beautiful pass accepted.

parks.name: Bryce Canyon
parks.overview: Bryce Canyon is not actually a canyon but a series of giant natural amphitheaters filled with thousands of hoodoos—tall, thin spires of rock eroded from the Paunsaugunt Plateau. The park sits at 8,000–9,100 ft elevation and offers one of the darkest, clearest night skies in the American Southwest, designated as an International Dark Sky Park.
highlights: Queen's Garden and Navajo Loop combination
Rim Trail between Bryce Point and Inspiration Point
Stargazing (one of the best dark-sky locations in the US)
Wall Street slot canyon in Navajo Loop

best_seasons.notes: The park is beautiful year-round. Summer can be hot at canyon floor but cool on the rim (8,000 ft). Winter brings snow that settles into the hoodoos for stunning white-and-orange photos. Snowshoe rentals available.

must_see_features: Watch sunrise from Bryce Point or Inspiration Point as the hoodoos glow orange
Descend the Navajo Loop through Wall Street's towering walls
Combine Navajo Loop and Queen's Garden for the best below-rim hike
Attend a ranger-led stargazing program (June–September)
Walk the Rim Trail at golden hour from Sunrise Point to Sunset Point

trails.name: Rim Trail
trails.notes: Flat paved trail along the rim; shuttle stops; accessible sections

trails.name: Navajo Loop
trails.notes: Descends 550 ft through Wall Street; steep but short; one of the most popular in the park

trails.name: Queens Garden + Navajo Loop
trails.notes: The classic combination; figure-eight through the best hoodoos below the rim

trails.name: Fairyland Loop
trails.notes: Less crowded; outstanding hoodoo scenery; involves 1,700 ft elevation change

wildlife.notes: Utah prairie dog towns are found throughout the park. California condors soar overhead—look for wing tags. The park's dark skies make nighttime wildlife observation unique.

entrance_fees.notes: 7-day pass. Free shuttle operates May–October between Bryce Canyon City and Ruby's Inn. America the Beautiful pass accepted.

parks.photo_credit: Photo: NPS / Bryce Canyon National Park

parks.name: Sequoia & Kings Canyon
parks.overview: Two neighboring parks managed together, Sequoia & Kings Canyon protect the largest trees on Earth by volume—the giant sequoia. General Sherman Tree is the world's largest living tree (by volume) at 52,500 cubic feet. Kings Canyon's steep-walled canyon rivals the Grand Canyon in depth, and the parks encompass the highest peaks in the contiguous US (Mt. Whitney, 14,505 ft).
highlights: General Sherman Tree (world's largest tree by volume)
Moro Rock (granite dome with panoramic views)
Mount Whitney (accessible from nearby Inyo NF)

best_seasons.notes: Kings Canyon Scenic Byway and Generals Highway fully open summer only; chain control required in winter on upper sections. Giant Forest Museum and General Sherman accessible year-round on Generals Highway.

must_see_features: Walk among the giant sequoias of the Giant Forest Grove to General Sherman Tree
Hike up Moro Rock steps for 360° views of the Great Western Divide
Take a ranger-led tour of Crystal Cave (reservations required)
Drive Kings Canyon Scenic Byway to Roads End and hike to Zumwalt Meadow
See General Grant Tree (the Nation's Christmas Tree)

trails.name: Congress Trail
trails.notes: Loop through the Giant Forest; passes General Sherman and dozens of massive sequoias

trails.name: Moro Rock
trails.notes: 350 stairs to a granite dome summit; panoramic views

trails.name: Zumwalt Meadow Loop
trails.notes: Flat meadow loop with views of Kings Canyon walls

trails.name: High Sierra Trail
trails.notes: One of the great trails of the Sierra Nevada; permit required; leads to Mt. Whitney

wildlife.notes: Black bears are common in campgrounds. Use bear canisters or food lockers at all times. The park has a robust bear management program—your cooperation is essential.

entrance_fees.notes: Combined Sequoia & Kings Canyon entrance fee covers both parks for 7 days. America the Beautiful pass accepted.

parks.photo_credit: Photo: NPS / Sequoia & Kings Canyon NPs

parks.name: Joshua Tree
parks.overview: Joshua Tree sits at the convergence of two distinct desert ecosystems—the Mojave and the Colorado—creating a uniquely bizarre and beautiful landscape. The namesake Joshua trees (Yucca brevifolia) twist and reach across the Mojave section while enormous boulder formations create a surreal playground for rock climbers and stargazers alike.
highlights: Joshua tree forests of the Mojave Desert section
Keys View (panoramic desert panorama to the Salton Sea)

best_seasons.notes: Spring wildflower season (late February–April) is magical when conditions align. Summer temperatures regularly exceed 110°F—dangerous without preparation. Fall is warm but manageable. Winter nights are cold but days are mild and uncrowded.

must_see_features: Walk the Cap Rock Nature Trail through Joshua tree forest and boulders
Drive Geology Tour Road (dirt road, high-clearance recommended) through desert lowlands
Visit Cholla Cactus Garden at late afternoon light
Drive to Keys View for sunset over the Coachella Valley
Attend a ranger-led night sky program (October–April) or stargaze from Skull Rock

trails.name: Barker Dam Nature Trail
trails.notes: Historic dam with a seasonal water pool; bighorn sheep sightings

trails.name: Skull Rock Nature Trail
trails.notes: Interpretive trail through boulder formations and the famous skull-shaped rock

trails.name: Ryan Mountain
trails.notes: Panoramic 360° views; exposed summit; excellent sunrise location

trails.name: Lost Palms Oasis
trails.notes: Desert wash leads to largest fan palm oasis in the park; bring extra water

wildlife.notes: Desert tortoise is a protected species—do not pick them up. If you see one on a road, gently move it in the direction it was headed. Bighorn sheep frequent the Barker Dam area.

entrance_fees.notes: 7-day pass. America the Beautiful pass accepted.

parks.name: Denali
parks.overview: Denali is home to North America's highest peak (20,310 ft / 6,190 m) and encompasses six million acres of wild Alaska interior. The only road into the park (Denali Park Road) is restricted to park buses beyond Savage River, preserving an extraordinary wilderness that supports grizzly bears, wolves, Dall sheep, caribou herds, and moose in nearly pristine subarctic conditions.
highlights: Denali peak (20,310 ft, highest in North America)

best_seasons.notes: The park is only fully accessible mid-May through mid-September. Denali is cloud-covered about 70% of summer days—a clear view of the peak is a gift. Midnight sun in June allows 24-hour photography. September brings fall colors and dramatic light.

must_see_features: Take a park bus to Eielson Visitor Center for your best chance to see the peak
Spot grizzly bears, moose, caribou, and Dall sheep from the bus (all are common)
Hike off-trail from Savage River to a ridgeline for unobstructed views
Visit Wonder Lake at midnight in June for reflection shots of Denali
Attend a sled dog demonstration at park headquarters (genuine working sled dogs)

trails.name: Savage River Loop
trails.notes: Accessible by car; first look at the Alaska Range; good for wildlife watching

trails.name: Horseshoe Lake
trails.notes: Near park entrance; beaver dams, waterfowl

trails.name: Triple Lakes Trail
trails.notes: Requires park bus to trailhead; subarctic lakes and ridge views

trails.name: Off-trail ridge hikes (permitted throughout the park)
trails.notes: No trail system beyond front country; use topo maps; permit required for overnight; technical zones require climbing registration

wildlife.notes: Denali's wildlife is world-class. The subarctic ecosystem is relatively intact. Bears are common throughout—bear spray is essential. The Toklat River area is a prime grizzly spot.

entrance_fees.notes: Park bus tickets ($36.50–$59.75 round-trip depending on destination) are required to travel beyond Savage River. Reservations open in December for the following summer. America the Beautiful pass covers entry fee but NOT bus tickets.
